The test fails, and nothing is retried, when: lifetime 1 does not return normally (the watchdog resets it, or its report has reason other than 0); lifetime 1 returns but the card did not switch (card_signals_1v8 false, outcome declined), in which case lifetime 2 is not run; lifetime 2 stops at identification (reason 3): the card did not answer at 1.8 V, so it refuses CMD0 re-entry, and the SD on this board stays unusable until power is removed.
conclusion:
Everything ran and the close failed; the lifetime did not return. Its fault record decodes, through the probe's stop word, as: reason 11 (the close failed), platform fault 1, platform stage 18 (CLOSE_WAIT), probe stage 8 (the end of the plan), 32 reads done. Identification, the switch (CMD11 on the card, bank to 1.8 V), 32 SDR25 reads and the capture all completed, the card clock was stopped, the bank was written back to 3.3 V and seen to report it (CLOSE_BANK finished), and the next stage failed a check. The report was written to RAM and lost, because a lifetime that cannot close cannot return.
Cause, found from lifetime 2's stop word (entry 1793649204965774597-d1ed3e86): the native adapter's register filter refused the close's last write, the restore of the inherited module setting. Its terminal-close exception named the high-speed profile only; in the UHS-I profile the setting had to be one of the three running settings, so update() failed in CLOSE_WAIT (platform source line 838, stage 18). The platform models write registers through their own hook, not the adapter's filter, so no host check applied the rule (the same gap as the first CMD25, recorded in storage-host-coverage-gap). The rule is now one pure function (a733_mmc_platform_native_module_write_allowed) that the adapter and the models both apply: the close restore is admitted for the high-speed and UHS-I profiles only with the module off and the bus in reset. checks/sd-return-close.c asserts it on every module write of a close, and checks/a733-mmc-native-filter.c tests it directly; the old rule fails both. A first hypothesis, that the withstand-mode word changes with the supply, also stopped the model in CLOSE_WAIT; a relaxation for it was added and removed when the real cause was found, because nothing showed the board does that.
A failed lifetime carries its site: the stop word published in the fault record's esr is the platform's fault line (10 bits), why (2), platform stage (5), S18A, the five speed-mode support bits, whether the card signals 1.8 V, and a fold of the 32 read CRCs; the site byte is the probe's reason. apps/sd-backup-probe/input.py stop --site N --esr W decodes it. The report keeps the same word and the platform's fault line, why, stage and the withstand mode word at identification and after the close. A lifetime that has not closed cannot return its report, by design: the SD controller, pins and bank are still held, so the stop word is what a failed close can publish.

Stop word 0x8a070000, site 3 (the probe's identification stage), decodes (with the layout in force at that image, the fields of a reason-11 word) to platform source line 552, why 0, platform stage 14 (IDENTIFY), no S18A, no card. Line 552 in a733_mmc_platform.c is where the platform sees the core in its FAULT state; the platform records the line of the first fail() and why 0 means no deadline, so no platform callback failed first and the platform's own deadline had not passed: the core faulted by itself. The bank had already moved to 1.8 V (stage 14 follows ENTER_1V8) and the SDR25 re-entry had worked on the same path, so the fault lies in what the trial adds after ACMD6: the CMD6 SDR104 check and set, the module clock change, the register programming or the CMD19 sweep (stage IDENTIFY spans everything from CMD0 to the card being ready for reads; the stop was not before CMD6). State left: the card at 1.8 V (possibly with SDR104 selected; CMD0 at 1.8 V ends that), the bank at 1.8 V until the watchdog reset, the board back in FEL.
Host reproduction: the model's failing sample delays produced three kinds of error (data CRC, wrong pattern, no data), all of which the core tolerates. The vendor driver counts every sampling error as a failed delay (SDXC_INTERRUPT_ERROR_BIT), among them the FIFO run error (bit 11), start-bit and end-bit errors. With a card model whose failing delays include a FIFO run error, the core faults in the sweep at the first such delay: state FAULT, error CONTROLLER, protocol step P_SD_TUNE, sample delay 3, which is what the platform saw. The core's TUNE_TOLERATED mask omitted bit 11; it was extended (bit 12, hardware locked, stays terminal) and the card model's terminal error in the sweep became bit 12. The cause on the board is inferred from that reproduction, not observed, because the stop word did not carry the core's error or step. The probe now publishes, for a lifetime that fails before identification, the core's error (4 bits), its protocol step (6) and half the sample delay it had reached (5) next to the platform's line, why and stage (input.py stop --site 3); the models run the sweep with all five kinds of sampling error.

| Per-request rate | | first 32 requests median 2.51 ms = 52.2 MB/s (SDR25: 6.1 ms, 21.4 MB/s); all 512 median 2.76 ms = 47.6 MB/s; 25% of the later requests take 5 to 17 ms |
| Sustained over 64 MiB | at least 45 MB/s at 150 MHz; 55 to 70 expected | 27.4 MB/s (2.446 s): below the threshold |
| Close | selector to 3.3 V, normal return | bank 3.3 V (value 2, selector 1), normal return |
The 55 to 70 MB/s prediction was too high for this card. The 512 requests add up to 2.10 s (mean 4.1 ms; median 2.76 ms); the probe's own gap between requests (take, CRC, submit, one task step each) adds 0.34 s (0.67 ms per request). A quarter of the requests take 5 to 17 ms, which is the card (a 2020 Phison SD32G) stalling on its media, not the bus: the requests that run clean complete at 47 to 52 MB/s, against a raw limit of 75 MB/s at 150 MHz. An OS loader that overlaps requests would recover the 0.34 s of gaps but not the card's stalls: about 30 MB/s sustained on this card, against 21.7 MB/s at 50 MHz (14.4 MB/s sustained by the same probe over 4 MiB). The gain from SDR104 on this card is 1.4 to 2.4 times, depending on whether the stalls count.
narrative:
Where the 5 to 17 ms requests are, from the 512 requests already measured. Requests are 128 KiB from sector 0 on, so request n starts at n x 128 KiB; 32 requests make one 4 MiB allocation unit. Of the 512, 127 took over 5 ms:
| Requests | Span | Time per request | Note |
| 0 to 7 | first 1 MiB | 9.3 to 17.4 ms | cold start: the SDR25 run's first 8 requests on the same sectors took 12.8 to 21.0 ms against 6.1 ms after, the same extra time (6.7 to 14.9 ms) at 50 and at 150 MHz |
| 8 to 384 | 1 MiB to 48 MiB | 2.43 to 2.80 ms, flat, 2.51 ms in the first AU, 2.76 ms after | clean: 47 to 52 MB/s |
| 385 to 511 | 48 MiB to 64 MiB | 5.0 to 17.4 ms, 5.1, 7.5, 10.0, 12.4 ms recurring | 119 of 127 requests; a few clean ones between |
Not periodic: the stalls are one block of 8 at the start and one zone from request 385 on (119 of its 127 requests slow, in runs of 67, 8, 22, 16, 5 and 1), not spaced by the 512 KiB, 1 MiB, 2 MiB or 4 MiB position (counts by position are flat), not at allocation-unit boundaries (AU 0 stalls in 8 of 32 requests, AUs 1 to 11 in none, AUs 12 to 15 in 28 to 32 of 32), and not after a fixed count of requests or bytes apart from the one change at 48 MiB. Not the bus: the extra time of the first eight requests is the same in absolute terms at SDR25 and SDR104. Quantised: in the slow zone the times cluster at 2.5 ms plus multiples of about 2.5 ms (5.1, 7.5, 10.0, 12.4), so the card inserts waits in steps. Not data content: the slow requests are mostly blocks of zeros (constant CRC 0x7ee8cdcd: 125 of the 127) and fast requests include 263 of the 265 non-constant blocks. The pattern follows the address (a slow first MiB, a fast 1 to 48 MiB, a slow 48 MiB onwards) and the time is independent of the bus speed: a card behaviour tied to regions of the flash translation or the card's read-ahead. What it cannot separate is the card's cost per command (a read-ahead that does not carry across our CMD12 and next CMD18) from its cost per byte of media. The SDR25 64 MiB run was never made, so whether the slow zone is slow at 50 MHz is not known; only the first 4 MiB were read there.
note: SDR104 at 150 MHz works: sweep window 16-63 (58 of 64 delays pass), chosen delay 40, 512 requests with no error and the first 32 CRCs equal to the SDR25 CRCs, normal close with the bank back at 3.3 V. Per-request median 47.6 MB/s (first 32: 52.2) against 21.4 at SDR25; sustained 27.4 MB/s over 64 MiB because 25% of requests stall 5 to 17 ms on the card, plus 0.67 ms of probe gap per request: the sustained threshold is missed. Queue outcome result-mismatch only because the text expectation is the older probe's.

hypothesis: Request-pattern experiment on 3-3: re-entry, SDR104, eight read phases.
conclusion: First submission of the request-pattern experiment stopped in the sweep, before any phase. Stop word 0x8a071c06, site 3, decoded with the identification layout: platform stage 14, source line 552, core error 3 (TIMEOUT), core protocol step 32 (P_SD_TUNE_RECOVER), sample delay reached 12 or 13. The sweep had reached its first failing delays and the recovery after a failed CMD19 waited more than 10 ms for the command or data state machine to finish, then gave up with TIMEOUT. The previous trial recovered from the same delays (10 to 15 failed there), so the controller's behaviour at the marginal delays is not repeatable: sometimes the command never completes. The recovery waited and reset afterwards; the vendor driver resets the host after every failed tuning command. The host model gained a failing delay that leaves the command stuck until a controller reset; the old recovery times out on it as the board's did, and the recovery now forces the reset (capped at 12 in a sweep, then TIMEOUT). No phase ran and no report exists. The card was left at 1.8 V (the lifetime never closed), the bank at 1.8 V until the watchdog reset, the board returned to FEL.
note: Stopped in the CMD19 sweep before any phase: stop word 0x8a071c06 site 3, core TIMEOUT in the post-failure recovery (P_SD_TUNE_RECOVER) at sample delay 12 or 13, platform stage IDENTIFY. The first trial recovered from the same delays; the recovery waited 10 ms for a command that never completed and gave up.

hypothesis: Request-pattern experiment on 3-3 with the recovery matched to the vendor's.
conclusion: Second submission of the request-pattern experiment stopped in the sweep at delay 16 or 17. Stop word 0x8a073be8, site 3: core error 7 (CARD), step P_SD_TUNE, delay 16 or 17, platform stage IDENTIFY. With the recovery matched to the vendor's (reset at once), the sweep got past delays 12 and 13, where the previous submission had stopped, and stopped later, on a delay that the first successful trial had passed. The core faulted when a command's R1 response carried a card status error (CARD_ERRORS), at the response of any command with data and again in the P_SD_TUNE step. After a transfer aborted by a controller reset the card reports COM_CRC_ERROR once in its next response (modelled; inferred, not observed). The board kernel's loop does not look at R1 at all: it judges a delay by the host's command and data errors and the pattern compare. The core now does the same in the sweep, and the tolerated sampling errors were the vendor's whole error set (bits 1, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15) plus data starvation (bit 10); only card insert and remove (bit 18, bit 31) stayed terminal (later replaced by the single rule of sd-uhs-recovery-tuning-audit). The card model's failing delays gained a hardware-locked and a starvation error, and a response with COM_CRC_ERROR after an aborted command: with the old core they fault, with the new one the sweep completes with the same window. This was the third stop in the sweep, each on a difference from the vendor loop that the host model did not have.
note: Stopped in the sweep at delay 16 or 17: stop word 0x8a073be8 site 3, core CARD error at P_SD_TUNE (a card status error in a CMD19 response), no phase ran. The vendor loop does not judge R1 status. Fixed in the core and the models.

hypothesis: Request-pattern experiment on 3-3: re-entry, SDR104, eight read phases (A to H), after the tuning-path audit.
prediction:
Request-pattern experiment (approved, one run): one lifetime, re-entry then SDR104 as before (--uhs-mode 3), then eight phases over the slow zone and controls (--phase FIRST:BLOCKS:READS[:quick]; quick skips the per-request CRC and the progress call except every 32nd request, bringing the gap between requests down from about 0.67 ms to what the platform's take and submit need).
| Phase | Region | Request | Count | Mode | Asks |
| A | 48 to 64 MiB | 128 KiB | 128 | normal | the zone again |
| B | the same | 128 KiB | 128 | quick | does the gap matter, or the second pass |
| C | the same | 128 KiB | 128 | normal | third pass: if slow again, B was the gap; if fast, the card remembers |
| D | the same | 64 KiB | 256 | normal | request size down |
| E | the same | 32 KiB | 512 | normal | request size down again |
| F | 4 to 12 MiB | 128 KiB | 64 | normal | the fast zone as a control |
| G | 100 to 116 MiB | 128 KiB | 128 | normal | an unseen region |
| H | 200 to 216 MiB | 128 KiB | 128 | quick | another unseen region, back to back |
Requests of 1 MiB and 4 MiB per CMD18 are not in it: the descriptor ring holds 33 descriptors, so a command reads at most 256 sectors (128 KiB), and larger sizes need the ring, the buffers and the platform's chain check extended; if the result points at the per-command cost they are the next step.
Prediction: a card behaviour that costs time per command, not per byte, and that our pattern does not cause. A: slow as before, mean 6 to 10 ms per request, 14 to 20 MB/s. B and C: the same as A within 20 percent (no gap or second-pass effect); if B is much faster than A and C slow again, the gap provokes it; if B and C are both fast, the card remembers. D and E: the per-command extra time stays about the same, so time per MiB rises: D about 1.5 to 1.8 times A per MiB, E about 2.5 to 3.5 times; if the time per MiB equals A's, the cost is per byte of media. F: fast, 2.4 to 2.8 ms per 128 KiB, 47 to 54 MB/s. G and H: slow like A (the zone beyond 48 MiB is where files lie), with H equal to G. No error in any phase; normal close; normal return. A clear difference between A and B or C, or D and E not rising, points at something our pattern does (or a media-bound card); a rise in D and E with B equal to A points at the per-command cost.
conclusion:
The sweep completed (passing delays 0 to 9 and 17 to 63, window 17 to 63, delay 40, 150 MHz; commit 1907eb70, image 851a4859). All 1,472 requests ran, the lifetime closed with the bank back at 3.3 V, and the board returned normally. The entry's result-mismatch is the placeholder expectation of the probe's input, not a run failure. Per phase (16 MiB for A to E, 8 MiB for F, G and H; mean request time, requests over 5 ms):
| Phase | Request | Region | Mean | Over 5 ms | Predicted |
| A | 128 KiB | 48 MiB, normal | 5.27 ms | 68 of 128 | 6 to 10 ms (missed: lower) |
| B | 128 KiB | same, quick | 5.42 ms | 70 of 128 | within 20 percent of A (met) |
| C | 128 KiB | same, normal again | 6.73 ms | 93 of 128 | within 20 percent of A (missed: 28 percent more) |
| D | 64 KiB | same | 4.82 ms (1.83 times A per MiB) | 88 of 256 | 1.5 to 1.8 times (just over) |
| E | 32 KiB | same | 1.93 ms (1.47 times A per MiB) | 9 of 512 | 2.5 to 3.5 times (missed) |
| F | 128 KiB | 4 MiB | 2.44 ms, every request | 0 | 2.4 to 2.8 ms (met) |
| G | 128 KiB | 100 MiB | 3.21 ms | 11 of 128 | slow like A (missed: mostly fast) |
| H | 128 KiB | 200 MiB, quick | 6.66 ms | 115 of 128 | slow like A (met) |
First, our request pattern is not the cause: the slow requests are the same requests in A, B and C (67 of the 68 slow ones in A are slow in B and in C), and quick or normal makes no difference (A against B). Second, a per-command cost is refuted: E issues four times as many commands as A over the same 16 MiB, and its extra time over the fast path is about the same in total (0.64 ms per request over 512 requests, 330 ms; A: 2.5 ms over 128 requests, 320 ms), where the per-command hypothesis predicted 2.5 to 3.5 times. Third, the slowness depends on the card's position and history together, not on the data: in A the slow requests are numbers 1 to 16 and 71 to 127 of the 48 to 64 MiB region and requests 17 to 70 are fast, yet D reading the first 8 MiB of the same region is slow from its third request to its last, and C's slow start extends to request 42 where A's ended at 16. The region is all zeros (the slow and fast requests have the same CRC). Fourth, regions differ: 4 MiB (F) is always fast, 100 MiB (G) mostly fast, 200 MiB (H) and 48 MiB (A to C) mostly slow. A fast request costs 2.75 ms for 128 KiB (47.6 MB/s), 1.81 ms for 64 KiB and 1.29 ms for 32 KiB, about 0.8 ms per command plus 16 us per KiB. Not explained: what in the card makes position 56 to 64 MiB slow in A to C but 48 to 56 MiB slow in D, and the changing length of the slow start; the candidates are the card's internal mapping lookups or read-ahead after a jump back (D, and each phase's start, follows a seek), which a descending or interleaved order would separate from position. The sustained figure over all eight phases is 20.4 MB/s, so on this card at this position mix SDR104 delivers about what SDR25 did; the 47.6 MB/s per request is reached only on fast regions.
note: Complete lifetime, normal return, bank back at 3.3 V; result-mismatch is the placeholder expectation, not the run. Slow requests are the same requests in A, B and C (67 of 68), quick or normal alike.

hypothesis: A strict model of a layer's core driven through its own callbacks proves the core against the protocol but not the platform layer that admits the core's accesses.
narrative: The platform's admission of the bounded write had no host coverage until checks/a733-mmc-platform-write.py. The strict CMD25 model (checks/sunxi-mmc-write-dma.c) drives the core with the model's own callbacks, so it never ran the platform's descriptor-chain check (dma_chain in drivers/storage/a733_mmc_platform.c), which refused every write-direction command. The first board writes, runs v11 and v12, stopped there: the controller was retained with no refused register and no deadline. The class of gap is a strict model tested with its own callbacks instead of the platform's: the model proves the core against the protocol and proves nothing about the layer that admits the core's accesses. A model of a layer's callee must be driven through that layer. checks/a733-mmc-platform-write.py runs the same model through the platform's core callbacks and the native adapter's register filter with a verified bounds object, and checks/a733-mmc-dma-chain.py pins the predicate; both fail on the platform source of v12. The same check applies to any other service that gets a strict model for its core. The same gap hid the UHS-I close failure (entry 1793648082135831049-05f70d50).

hypothesis: Throughput figures measured with the SD0 interrupt disabled do not describe the card or the driver.
narrative: Until the fix that sets GCTRL bit 4 with the interrupt mask (the board kernel's global interrupt enable, sunxi_mmc_init_host), the SD0 interrupt never reached the owner and every wait for a transfer ended on the 5 ms recheck timer. The earlier write throughput (368 MiB in at most 40 s, about 9.2 MiB/s, which included stream generation), the read rate of the mode 2 runs (6.1 MB/s over 232 MiB, 5.4 ms per request; entry 1793631795893042045-0c63a1cc) and any per-request latency from the runs before the fix are therefore not the card's or the driver's rates. They are superseded by the runs of the image with the interrupt enabled (entries 1793632286777262813-62b0f3bb and 1793632378497932347-1618d4a8); the result then carries irq_entries per core and owner_recheck_wakes, which should be about one per request and about zero. The 21.9 MB/s read figure of the standalone probe (entry 1793602100319385552-a0551753) was measured by polling and is unaffected.

hypothesis: Sequential reads through the file API resolve the path once and walk each cluster link at most once.
prediction: Reads through the file API were quadratic in file size, because fwr_read resolved the path, scanned the directory and walked the chain from the first cluster on every call. 5,888 reads of 64 KiB over the 368 MiB file did not finish in 52 s (entry 1793625959251868124-3ed648e5). struct fwr_cursor and fwr_read_cursor (include/fat32_rw.h) keep the file's first cluster, size and the cluster of the last byte read, so a sequential read continues from there and a read behind it walks from the start; ss_read keeps one cursor per descriptor. Any directory write on the volume bumps a generation count that makes the cursor resolve again, so it never serves a stale size or chain. checks/fat32-read-cursor.py requires one resolution and at most one link per cluster crossed, and the data to match after an append, a replace and an unlink.
conclusion: Host result: 511 and 2,047 links for 256 KiB and 1 MiB, against 67,667 and 1,075,100 without the cursor. Not run on the board: the application's verify still reads in 4 MiB steps with fwr_read until it is switched to the cursor.

hypothesis: The write service is board-qualified for bounded writes on the 62.5 GB card through the OS image's SD owner task.
narrative:
Card: 62.5 GB, Class 10, U3, V30, A1, 4 MiB allocation unit; profile 2 (high speed, four-bit, 50 MHz); the runner admits a blob that names every write and backup range.
Bounded writes: a 512 MiB file /sunstone-test/sunstone-region-test.bin created in a preallocated, contiguous chain (cluster 47 to 16430), verified end to end by a read-only open (mode 3, 0 mismatches) and by the read-only probe (chain whole, FAT copies equal, FAT[1] clean, FSInfo as predicted).
Append: 144 MiB appended to the existing file in a later session with the same checks; the file reached its full size with the chain extended and FSInfo, directory entry and both FAT copies consistent.
Interruption and recovery: the OS ended a session at its own deadline in the middle of a flush while the application wrote a new file with a sync every 8 MiB (entry 1793635810117434075-86ece323). The card was left with FAT[1] dirty, the new file's entry at 40 MiB (five syncs), a chain of 1,280 clusters and FSInfo unchanged, with the unsynced clusters unlinked (1793635995914258228-cb1f4fc3). The next session mounted with the writer enabled; recovery ran once, wrote 1,536 bytes of metadata (the FAT copies and FSInfo), set FAT[1] clean, and the 40 MiB file read back with 0 mismatches (1793636210564944400-a065537e). The probe after recovery (1793636300522250962-f6977cff) and the region file read (1793636342034468404-7527d869: 512 MiB, 0 mismatches, no card write) closed the sequence. Recovery left the FSInfo next-free hint at 4, the lowest free cluster; it is now the first free cluster after the highest used one (or the old hint while it is still free), checked by checks/fat32-rw.py.
Throughput: reads 21.7 MB/s (6.0 ms per 128 KiB request); writes 14.7 MB/s flushed (about 8 ms per 128 KiB piece; flush latency p50 256 ms, p99 803 ms), both with the interrupt enabled, at the top CPU point.
Not qualified: more than one interruption point (the host power-loss sweep covers every sector write; the board has one cut), other cards, writes outside /sunstone-test/, directories other than the existing one, and concurrent writers.
